def-dep-breakdown.title: Breakdown point
def-dep-breakdown.html: Let T be an estimator that maps a data set Z of n cases (x(i),yi) to a vector in Rp. For m≤n, let b(m;T,Z) be the supremum of ‖T(Z′)−T(Z)‖ over all data sets Z′ obtained from Z by replacing any m of its cases with arbitrary values, for which T(Z′) is defined. The finite-sample breakdown point of T at Z is ε∗(T,Z)=min{mn: b(m;T,Z)=∞}.

exm-dep-along-across.title: Predicting along and across the pattern
exm-dep-along-across.title_html: Predicting along and across the pattern
exm-dep-along-across.html: Draw m=40 pairs of regressors with sample correlation 0.9868, so that each has a variance inflation factor of 38.1, and fit E(Y)=β0+β1x1+β2x2. In units of σ, the two slopes have standard deviations 0.904 and 0.907. At the new point (x1,x2)=(1,1), which follows the pattern of the data, the fitted mean has standard deviation 0.228, close to the root mean square over the design points, 3/40=0.274. At (1,−1), which is just as far from the origin but against the pattern, it is 1.809. Figure 19.6.1 shows the contours of this standard deviation. They are long ellipses aligned with the data cloud.

exm-dep-ar1.title: A trend with autocorrelated errors
exm-dep-ar1.html:
Take n=20 equally spaced times and errors with vst=ρ|s−t|, the covariance of a stationary first-order autoregression, with ρ=0.6. Fit a straight line in two designs, a linear trend xt=t and an alternating regressor xt=(−1)t. For the trend, the expected usual variance of the slope is 0.256 times its true variance, so the root of the expected usual variance is 0.506 of the true standard error. Yet ordinary least squares is nearly efficient: generalized least squares has 0.905 of its variance. For the alternating regressor the error goes the other way. The ratio is 3.271, so the standard error is too large by a factor 1.809, and the efficiency is 0.950. Swindel’s bounds for this V are 0.193 and 4.31, so both designs lie well towards the extremes. The Kantorovich bound, 0.2351 from λ1=3.757 and λn=0.2514, is far below either efficiency.

In 100000 simulated series with normal errors, the nominal 95% t interval for the slope covered the true value in 0.693 of them for the trend and 0.9976 for the alternating regressor. Figure 19.2.1 shows the whole range of ρ.

exm-dep-coverage.title: Coverage of the t interval
exm-dep-coverage.html:
Fit a straight line with normal, centred exponential and scaled t(3) errors, each with variance one, in two designs. In the spread design x=1,…,n, and hn∗ is 0.345, 0.096 and 0.025 at n=10, 40 and 160. In the far-point design the last value is moved to x=4n, and hn∗ is 0.954, 0.800 and 0.485. With 100000 data sets per case, the coverages of the nominal 95% interval for the slope are:

Design Errors n=10 n=40 n=160
spread normal 0.950 0.951 0.950
spread exponential 0.955 0.953 0.950
spread t(3) 0.955 0.952 0.951
far point normal 0.951 0.950 0.951
far point exponential 0.933 0.948 0.950
far point t(3) 0.931 0.944 0.953

The two-sided coverages hide unbalanced tails. With exponential errors and the far point, the interval misses above the slope in 0.067 of the data sets at n=10 and below it in only 0.001. At n=160 the two proportions are 0.038 and 0.012, still far from 0.025 each, as the slowly falling leverage predicts. A one-sided test in this design has nearly three times its nominal size at n=10. Panel (a) of Figure 19.3.1 shows the skewed t statistic at n=40. The t(3) errors have no fourth moment, but @thm-dep-nonnormal still applies.

exm-dep-curved-mean.title: A line through a parabola
exm-dep-curved-mean.html:
Let X be uniform on (0,2), E(Y∣X)=X2 and Var(Y∣X)=0.04, with normal errors. A straight line is fitted. The population line has slope β∗=Cov(X,X2)/Var(X)=2 and intercept −2/3, and the approximation error is U02−1/3 with U0=X−1 uniform on (−1,1). The slope’s component of Σ−1ΩΣ−1 is E[(X−1)2U2]/Var(X)2 (@exr-dep-slope-sandwich), which equals 9(44/945+0.04/3)=0.5390. The usual formula estimates E(U2)/Var(X)=3(4/45+0.04)=0.3867 instead. The true standard error is 1.181 times what the usual one estimates, and by @thm-dep-random-x(c) the nominal 95% interval for β∗ has limiting coverage 0.903.

Simulation agrees. With 40000 samples the interval covered β∗=2 in 0.896 of samples of size 50 and 0.900 of size 400; with 10000 samples of size 1600, in 0.908. Over the same samples, n times the variance of the slope was 0.584, 0.546 and 0.530, approaching the sandwich value 0.5390, not the usual 0.3867. As a statement about the design-dependent target 𝛃βX, the same intervals are conservative. They covered it in 0.999 of the samples of size 50, because s2 estimates E(U2)=0.1289 rather than σ2=0.04. In a larger simulation of 200000 samples of size 50, the variance of the slope, 0.01163, splits as in @prp-dep-design-target(b) into 0.00249 from the errors and 0.00913 from the variation of βX between designs.

exm-dep-equicorrelated.title: Equicorrelated errors
exm-dep-equicorrelated.html: Let V=(1−ρ)I+ρ11⊤, with −1/(n−1)<ρ<1 so that V is positive definite, and let the model contain an intercept, X=[1,X1]. It arises when all observations share one random shock. Since VX=(1−ρ)X+ρ1(1⊤X) has columns in C(X), Kruskal’s condition holds and 𝛃β^ is the best linear unbiased estimator. Its covariance is not σ2(X⊤X)−1, however. Because Xe1=1 for the first standard basis vector e1, we have (X⊤X)−1X⊤1=e1, and @thm-dep-covariance(a) gives 𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2(1−ρ)(X⊤X)−1+σ2ρe1e1⊤. By @exr-rv-rss-correlated, E(s2)=σ2(1−ρ). So s2(X⊤X)−1 is exactly unbiased for the covariance of the slopes, whose information comes from comparisons in which the common shock cancels. For the intercept it misses the term σ2ρ. When ρ>0 this term does not shrink as n grows, so the intercept is not even consistent, and its reported standard error goes to zero anyway (@exr-dep-equicorrelated-intercept). The same holds for any fitted mean 𝛃x0⊤β^, since x0⊤e1=1 whenever x0 has a leading 1.

exm-dep-indicator.title: An observation with its own parameter
exm-dep-indicator.title_html: An observation with its own parameter
exm-dep-indicator.html: Fit an intercept together with an indicator of the first observation, Xn=[1,e1], so that h11=1 for every n. The least squares estimates are μ^=Y¯(1), the mean of observations 2,…,n, and δ^=Y1−Y¯(1). Hence δ^−δ=ε1−ε¯(1),Var(δ^)=σ2(1+1n−1), and since ε¯(1)→0 in probability, δ^−δ→ε1 in distribution. The limit is the error distribution itself. No amount of other data can average away the error of one observation.

exm-dep-longley.title: Longley’s regression
exm-dep-longley.html: Longley’s (1967) data, which @exm-cmp-longley used to test the accuracy of least squares algorithms, regress total employment on six economic series over n=16 years. The variance inflation factors range from 3.59 for ARMED (the size of the armed forces) to 1788.5 for GNP. The eigenvalues of the correlation matrix run from 4.603 down to 0.00038, and the factors sum to 3119.4, which is the sum of the reciprocal eigenvalues, as @prp-dep-collinear-directions(c) requires. Four of the series (the price deflator, GNP, population and the year itself) rose almost in step over the sixteen years, each with correlation above 0.99 with the year. The data can say much about their joint movement and almost nothing about any one of them with the others held fixed.

exm-dep-polynomial-risk.title: Choosing a polynomial degree
exm-dep-polynomial-risk.html: Part (c) of @thm-dep-mse applies to any nested sequence of models. Take n=40 equally spaced points on [−1,1], the mean μ(x)=exsin⁡3x, which is not a polynomial, and σ=0.25. A polynomial of degree d has p=d+1 columns, and its risk at the design points is 𝛍σ2(d+1)+‖(I−Md)μ‖2. Panel (b) of Figure 19.1.1 shows the two terms. In units of σ2 the risk is 161.41 for a straight line, falls to 5.52 at degree 4, and climbs back to 11.00 at degree 10, where the fit is almost unbiased and pays only for its variance. @exr-dep-add-one-term shows that adding one term lowers the risk iff that term’s own noncentrality exceeds 1.

exm-dep-short-wins.title: A biased estimator that wins
exm-dep-short-wins.html:
Take n=30 observations of two centred regressors with unit sample variances and sample correlation r=0.9, an intercept, σ=1 and β2=0.301, chosen so that γ=0.5. Here Π has slope entry r, so the short slope on x1 has bias rβ2=0.271. Its standard deviation is 0.186, against 0.426 for the long slope, and the ratio of mean squared error to long variance is 0.595. A simulation with 200000 data sets gives 0.594.

For two standardized regressors the ratio has a closed form (@exr-dep-two-regressors): E(β^1S−β1)2Var(β^1)=1−r2+r2γ=1+r2(γ−1),{#eq-dep-two-regressor-ratio}

which is 1−0.81+0.81×0.5=0.595. The short slope wins iff γ<1, as @thm-dep-mse(b) requires, and the stakes, gain or loss, are proportional to r2. This is panel (a) of Figure 19.1.1. The short model’s s12 has mean 1+γ/(n−2)=1.0179, a bias too small to notice.

exm-dep-stackloss.title: The last day of the stack loss data
exm-dep-stackloss.title_html: The last day of the stack loss data
exm-dep-stackloss.html:
In the stack loss data of @exm-opt-stackloss-mle, n=21 days of a plant oxidizing ammonia, regress the stack loss on air flow, water temperature and acid concentration with an intercept. The average leverage is p/n=0.190. By @eq-dep-influence, the case whose deletion moves the fitted vector most is day 21, with leverage 0.285 and residual −7.238. Deleting it moves the fitted vector by a distance of 5.396. The next largest move, for day 1, is 2.543, and the median over all days is 1.228. The largest leverage, 0.412 for day 17, comes with a residual of only −1.520, and that day has little influence.

Without day 21, the air-flow coefficient rises from 0.716 to 0.889, the water temperature coefficient falls from 1.295 to 0.817, and s drops from 3.243 to 2.569. The mean-shift estimate for day 21 is δ^=−10.116. The listing computes every deletion effect from the single fit (@thm-dep-outlier(c)).

Adding Δ=10 to the response of the lowest-leverage day, day 5 with h55=0.052, moves the fitted vector by 2.285 and its own residual by 9.478. The same shift on day 17 moves the fitted vector by 6.420 and its residual by only 5.879.

exr-dep-add-one-term.title: B3
exr-dep-add-one-term.html: Let C(X1)⊂C(X2)⊂⋯ be nested model spaces with dimensions p1<p2<⋯, and let 𝛍μ=E(Y) be arbitrary. Show that the risk 𝛍E‖MkY−μ‖2 of model k exceeds that of model k+1 iff 𝛍γk=‖(Mk+1−Mk)μ‖2/σ2>pk+1−pk.

exr-dep-bad-leverage.title: B1
exr-dep-bad-leverage.html: In a straight-line regression, move the x value of case k to t while keeping yk fixed. Show that the fitted slope tends to 0 as t→∞. If instead yk=ct+d moves with t, show that the slope tends to c.

exr-dep-berkson.title: B1
exr-dep-berkson.html: In the controlled-regressor model, let δi and εi be independent, with variances τ2 and σ2, independent of the settings. Show that least squares on the nominal xi is unbiased for (β0,β1), that the usual standard errors are valid with error variance σ2+β12τ2, and that s2 estimates this variance.

exr-dep-contamination-power.title: B2
exr-dep-contamination-power.html: Suppose case k is contaminated by Δ, and consider the t statistic for a coefficient βj whose estimate is unaffected, [(X⊤X)−1x(k)]j=0. Using @thm-dep-outlier(b), explain how the contamination still changes the test, and show that its effect on E(s2) is largest for low-leverage cases.

exr-dep-contrast-skewness.title: B1
exr-dep-contrast-skewness.html: In a one-way layout with m observations per group and skewed errors, compute ∑iwi3 of @prp-dep-cumulants for (i) a single group mean and (ii) the difference of two group means. What does this say about one-sample and two-sample t tests with skewed data?

exr-dep-convex-hull.title: C1
exr-dep-convex-hull.html: Show that if x0 is a convex combination of the rows of X, then 𝛃Var(x0⊤β^)≤σ2maxihii. Is the converse true: does a small prediction variance mean x0 lies inside the data? Compare with @exm-ci-hidden-extrapolation.

exr-dep-diagonal-s2.title: A1
exr-dep-diagonal-s2.html: Let V=diag(v1,…,vn). Show that E(s2)=σ2∑i(1−hii)vi/(n−p), a weighted average of the variances σ2vi.

exr-dep-equicorrelated-intercept.title: B2
exr-dep-equicorrelated-intercept.html: In @exm-dep-equicorrelated with ρ>0, show that Var(β^0)≥σ2ρ for every n, while E(v)→0 for the intercept when [(X⊤X)−1]11→0. Explain the result by writing εi=ρσZ+1−ρσUi with independent standardized Z,U1,…,Un.

exr-dep-far-leverage.title: A2
exr-dep-far-leverage.html: In the far-point design of @exm-dep-coverage, show that the leverage of the far point is approximately 147/(n+147) for large n. Why does the table still show nearly nominal two-sided coverage at n=160, when the leverage is almost one half?

exr-dep-hetero-clt.title: C1
exr-dep-hetero-clt.html: Let the errors be independent with mean zero, variances σi2∈[m0,M0] with m0>0, and supiE|εi|3<∞. Suppose hn∗→0. Show that for every nonzero an, 𝛃𝛃𝛃(an⊤β^−an⊤β)/Var(an⊤β^)→N(0,1), where the variance is the sandwich @eq-lm-sandwich. Explain why this does not make the usual t statistic asymptotically standard normal.

exr-dep-hetero-harmless.title: B2
exr-dep-hetero-harmless.html: In @thm-dep-random-x, show that Σ−1ΩΣ−1=E(U2)Σ−1 iff E[(E(U2∣x)−E(U2))xx⊤]=0. Give an example of a nonconstant E(U2∣x) for which the usual standard errors are nevertheless consistent.

exr-dep-hetero-origin.title: B1
exr-dep-hetero-origin.html: For the regression through the origin E(Yi)=βxi with Var(Yi)=σ2vi, show that Var(β^)=σ2∑ihivi/∑ixi2 and E(v)=σ2∑i(1−hi)vi/((n−1)∑ixi2), where hi=xi2/∑jxj2 are the leverages. Conclude that the usual standard error is too small on average iff the leverage-weighted average of the vi exceeds the (1−hi)-weighted average.

exr-dep-influence-function.title: C1
exr-dep-influence-function.html: Let (x,Y) have a joint distribution F with Σ=E(xx⊤) positive definite, and let 𝛃β∗(F)=Σ−1E(xY) be the population least squares coefficient. For the mixture Fϵ=(1−ϵ)F+ϵδ(x0,y0), which puts mass ϵ at a single point, show that 𝛃𝛃ddϵβ∗(Fϵ)|ϵ=0=Σ−1x0(y0−x0⊤β∗(F)), and compare with @thm-dep-outlier(c) for a sample of size n.

exr-dep-line-quadratic.title: A1
exr-dep-line-quadratic.html: A straight line is fitted at x=0,1,2,3 when the true mean is β0+β1x+β2x2. Find the biases of the fitted intercept and slope.

exr-dep-line-threshold.title: B1
exr-dep-line-threshold.html: In @exr-dep-line-quadratic, show that ‖(I−M1)X2‖2=4. For which values of β2/σ does the straight line have a smaller mean squared error matrix than the quadratic fit, in the sense of @thm-dep-mse(b)? For which values is it better at the four design points?

exr-dep-linear-target.title: A2
exr-dep-linear-target.html: In @prp-dep-design-target, show that 𝛃Cov(βX)=0 when 𝛍𝛃μ(X)=Xβ, and give an example of a nonlinear 𝛍μ for which 𝛃Cov(βX)=0 anyway.

exr-dep-median-breakdown.title: A1
exr-dep-median-breakdown.html: Show that the sample median of n numbers has breakdown point ⌊(n+1)/2⌋/n, in the sense of @def-dep-breakdown with p=1 and no regressors.

exr-dep-other-residuals.title: A2
exr-dep-other-residuals.html: In @thm-dep-outlier(a), show that the residual of every other case i moves by −Δmik, where mik is an entry of M. Which cases’ residuals are most affected by a contaminated high-leverage case?

exr-dep-s2-mse.title: C1
exr-dep-s2-mse.html: Assume normal errors. Compare s12 (short) and s2 (long) as estimators of σ2 by mean squared error, when 𝛃β2≠0. Show that s12 is better iff 2(n−p1)+4γ+γ2<2(n−p1)2/(n−p), and interpret the condition when n is large.

exr-dep-slope-sandwich.title: A1
exr-dep-slope-sandwich.html: With x=(1,X)⊤, show that the slope entries of Σ−1ΩΣ−1 and E(U2)Σ−1 are E[(X−μX)2U2]/Var(X)2 and E(U2)/Var(X).

exr-dep-spread-leverage.title: A1
exr-dep-spread-leverage.html: For a straight line at x=1,…,n, show that the largest leverage is 1/n+3(n−1)/(n(n+1))<4/n.

exr-dep-sum-difference.title: B1
exr-dep-sum-difference.html: For two centred regressors with ‖x1‖2=‖x2‖2=S and correlation r, show that Var(β^1+β^2)=2σ2/(S(1+r)) and Var(β^1−β^2)=2σ2/(S(1−r)). Relate the result to @prp-dep-collinear-directions(a) and to Figure 19.6.1.

exr-dep-swindel-attained.title: C1
exr-dep-swindel-attained.html: Show that both bounds of @thm-dep-covariance(d) are attained. Hint: take C(X) spanned by eigenvectors of V, and choose a so that u is one of them.

exr-dep-swindel-trivial.title: A2
exr-dep-swindel-trivial.html: Show that the bounds of @thm-dep-covariance(d) do not change when V is replaced by cV for c>0, and that both equal 1 iff V is a multiple of I.

exr-dep-two-components.title: C1
exr-dep-two-components.html: In @thm-dep-random-x, let E(Y∣x)=m(x), Var(Y∣x)=σ2, and put 𝛃d(x)=m(x)−x⊤β∗. Show that 𝛃𝛃n(βX−β∗)→Np(0,Σ−1E(d2xx⊤)Σ−1), and that Σ−1ΩΣ−1=σ2Σ−1+Σ−1E(d2xx⊤)Σ−1. Interpret the two terms in the light of @prp-dep-design-target(b).

exr-dep-two-regressors.title: B2
exr-dep-two-regressors.html: Derive @eq-dep-two-regressor-ratio. Take an intercept and two centred regressors with ‖x1‖2=‖x2‖2=S and sample correlation r. Show that Var(β^1)=σ2/(S(1−r2)), that the short slope has variance σ2/S and bias rβ2, and that γ=β22S(1−r2)/σ2.

exr-dep-uncorrelated-s2.title: A2
exr-dep-uncorrelated-s2.html: True or false: if the omitted regressors are orthogonal to the included ones (X1⊤X2=0), the short regression is harmless, including its estimate of σ2.

exr-dep-variance-ratio.title: B2
exr-dep-variance-ratio.html: Two independent samples of size m are each centred at their own mean. Let S12 and S22 be the sample variances. (i) Show that the vector d of @prp-dep-balance has entries 1/m and −1/m. (ii) Using the first part of @prp-dep-sigma-interval for each sample, show that when the two variances are equal the two-sided variance-ratio test of nominal size α has size tending to 2(1−Φ(zα/22/(2+κ))) as m→∞.

exr-dep-vif-bounds.title: B2
exr-dep-vif-bounds.html: Show that ∑jVIFj≥k, and that maxjVIFj≥(∑jVIFj)/k. Deduce that a correlation matrix with a small eigenvalue must have at least one large variance inflation factor, and conversely.

exr-dep-vif-inverse.title: A1
exr-dep-vif-inverse.html: Let Z be the n×k matrix of centred regressors, each scaled to unit length, so that Z⊤Z=R. Use @eq-proj-partitioned-inverse to show that [R−1]jj=1/(1−Rj2).

exr-dep-vif-one.title: A2
exr-dep-vif-one.html: Show that VIFj≥1, with equality iff the centred xj is orthogonal to every other centred regressor.

lem-dep-ky-fan.title: Trace of a compressed matrix
lem-dep-ky-fan.html: Let A be symmetric with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn, and let P be a symmetric idempotent matrix of rank k. Then ∑i=n−k+1nλi ≤ tr(PA) ≤ ∑i=1kλi.

lem-dep-rank-one.title: A rank-one comparison
lem-dep-rank-one.html: Let C be a positive definite q×q matrix, b∈Rq and c>0. Then cC−bb⊤ is nonnegative definite iff b⊤C−1b≤c.

lem-dep-short-long.title: Short and long regressions
lem-dep-short-long.html:
In this setting:

  1. 𝛃β^2=(X2⊤(I−M1)X2)−1X2⊤(I−M1)Y and 𝛃𝛃𝛃β^1=β^1S−Πβ^2;

  2. 𝛃𝛃Cov(β^1S,β^2)=0 and 𝛃Cov(β^2)=σ2C, where C=(X2⊤(I−M1)X2)−1.

lem-dep-weighted-clt.title: Weighted sums of errors
lem-dep-weighted-clt.html: Let wn=(wn1,…,wnn)⊤ be constant vectors with ‖wn‖=1 and mn=maxi|wni|→0. Then σ−1∑iwniεi→N(0,1) in distribution.

prp-dep-balance.title: Kurtosis and a ratio of mean squares
prp-dep-balance.title_html: Kurtosis and a ratio of mean squares
prp-dep-balance.html: Let P1 and P2 be symmetric idempotent with P1P2=0, ranks f1 and f2, and 𝛃𝛃P1Xβ=P2Xβ=0. Let the errors have finite fourth moment and excess kurtosis κ, put Sj2=Y⊤PjY/fj, and let pj be the vector of diagonal entries of Pj. Then L=(S12−S22)/σ2 has mean zero and Var(L)=2f1+2f2+κ‖d‖2,d=p1f1−p2f2. In particular, if both P1 and P2 have constant diagonals, then d=0 and Var(L) is the same as under normality.

prp-dep-breakdown.title: Least squares breaks down at one case
prp-dep-breakdown.title_html: Least squares breaks down at one case
prp-dep-breakdown.html: For least squares and every data set with a full-rank model matrix, ε∗=1/n.

prp-dep-collinear-directions.title: Where collinearity costs variance
prp-dep-collinear-directions.html:
Let X have full rank and let X⊤X=∑ℓ=1pλℓvℓvℓ⊤ with orthonormal eigenvectors vℓ and eigenvalues λℓ>0.

  1. For every a∈Rp, 𝛃Var(a⊤β^)=σ2∑ℓ(a⊤vℓ)2/λℓ.

  2. The fitted values at the design points have average variance σ2p/n, whatever the eigenvalues.

  3. With R as above, ∑jVIFj=trR−1=∑ℓ1/λℓ(R), and every VIFj≤1/λmin(R).

prp-dep-cumulants.title: Skewness and kurtosis of a linear estimate
prp-dep-cumulants.title_html: Skewness and kurtosis of a linear estimate
prp-dep-cumulants.html: Let the errors have finite fourth moment, skewness γ1=μ3/σ3 with μ3=E(εi3), and excess kurtosis κ. For a≠0 let 𝛃𝛃𝛃Z=(a⊤β^−a⊤β)/Var(a⊤β^), and let wi=ci/‖c‖ with c=X(X⊤X)−1a. Then E(Z3)=γ1∑iwi3,E(Z4)−3=κ∑iwi4, and |∑iwi3|≤h∗, ∑iwi4≤h∗, where h∗=maxihii.

prp-dep-design-target.title: The design-dependent target
prp-dep-design-target.html:
Let (X,Y) be random with rank(X)=p<n almost surely, 𝛍E(Y∣X)=μ(X) for some function 𝛍μ with values in Rn, not necessarily in C(X), and Cov(Y∣X)=σ2In. Put 𝛃𝛍βX=(X⊤X)−1X⊤μ(X).

  1. 𝛃𝛃E(β^∣X)=βX and 𝛃Cov(β^∣X)=σ2(X⊤X)−1.

  2. If the second moments below are finite, 𝛃𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2E[(X⊤X)−1]+Cov(βX).

  3. 𝛍E(s2∣X)=σ2+‖(I−M)μ(X)‖2/(n−p).

prp-dep-sigma-interval.title: The interval for sigma squared
prp-dep-sigma-interval.html:
In the sequence of models above, let the errors have finite fourth moment with κ>−2. Then n(s2/σ2−1)→N(0,2+κ), and the coverage of the nominal 1−α interval of @prp-ci-sigma tends to 2Φ(zα/22/(2+κ))−1,{#eq-dep-sigma-limit}

where Φ is the standard normal distribution function. The limit equals 1−α iff κ=0.

thm-dep-covariance.title: Least squares under a wrong covariance
thm-dep-covariance.title_html: Least squares under a wrong covariance
thm-dep-covariance.html:
Under @eq-dep-cov-model, let a∈Rp be nonzero and let v=s2a⊤(X⊤X)−1a be the usual estimate of 𝛃Var(a⊤β^).

  1. 𝛃𝛃E(β^)=β and 𝛃Cov(β^)=σ2(X⊤X)−1X⊤VX(X⊤X)−1.

  2. E(s2)=σ2tr((I−M)V)/(n−p).

  3. With u=X(X⊤X)−1a/‖X(X⊤X)−1a‖, a unit vector in C(X), 𝛃E(v)Var(a⊤β^)=tr((I−M)V)/(n−p)u⊤Vu.{#eq-dep-se-ratio}

  4. Let λ1≥⋯≥λn>0 be the eigenvalues of V, let λ¯− be the mean of the n−p smallest and λ¯+ the mean of the n−p largest. Then 𝛃λ¯−λ1≤E(v)Var(a⊤β^)≤λ¯+λn.

thm-dep-efficiency.title: Efficiency of least squares
thm-dep-efficiency.html: Under @eq-dep-cov-model, with λ1 and λn the largest and smallest eigenvalues of V, a⊤(X⊤V−1X)−1aa⊤(X⊤X)−1X⊤VX(X⊤X)−1a ≥ 4λ1λn(λ1+λn)2 for every a≠0. The bound is attained for p=1 and X=x=(q1+qn)/2, where q1,qn are unit eigenvectors for λ1,λn.

thm-dep-mse.title: When the short regression wins
thm-dep-mse.html:
In the setting of this section, let G=(−ΠIp2), a p×p2 matrix.

  1. The mean squared error matrix of 𝛃β^S is 𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃𝛃E[(β^S−β)(β^S−β)⊤]=Cov(β^)−G(σ2C−β2β2⊤)G⊤.

  2. 𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃𝛌𝛃E(λ⊤β^S−λ⊤β)2≤Var(λ⊤β^) for every 𝛌λ∈Rp iff γ≤1. If γ>1, the reverse strict inequality holds for some 𝛌λ.

  3. Over the design points, 𝛃𝛃E‖Xβ^S−Xβ‖2=σ2(p1+γ), against σ2p for the long fit. The short fit is better there iff γ<p2.

thm-dep-nonnormal.title: Least squares with nonnormal errors
thm-dep-nonnormal.html:
In the sequence of models above, suppose hn∗→0. Let s2=‖(I−M)Yn‖2/(n−p).

  1. For every sequence of nonzero vectors an∈Rp, 𝛃𝛃an⊤β^−an⊤βσan⊤(Xn⊤Xn)−1an ⟶ N(0,1)in distribution.

  2. s2→σ2 in probability. This part does not need hn∗→0.

  3. The t statistic, with s in place of σ in (a), tends to N(0,1), and the nominal 1−α interval 𝛃an⊤β^±tn−p,α/2san⊤(Xn⊤Xn)−1an has coverage tending to 1−α.

  4. Let Λ be a fixed p×q matrix of rank q, and suppose 𝛃Λ⊤β=d. The statistic 𝛃𝛃Fn=(Λ⊤β^−d)⊤[Λ⊤(Xn⊤Xn)−1Λ]−1(Λ⊤β^−d)qs2 satisfies qFn→χ2(q) in distribution, and Pr{Fn>Fα(q,n−p)}→α.

thm-dep-omitted.title: Omitted regressors
thm-dep-omitted.html:
Fit the short model when the long model is true.

  1. 𝛃𝛃𝛃E(β^1S)=β1+Πβ2 and 𝛃Cov(β^1S)=σ2(X1⊤X1)−1. The bias 𝛃Πβ2 vanishes iff 𝛃X1⊤X2β2=0, and it vanishes for every 𝛃β2 iff X1⊤X2=0.

  2. The fitted values have mean 𝛃𝛃Xβ−(I−M1)X2β2. The residuals have mean 𝛃(I−M1)X2β2 and covariance σ2(I−M1), as if the short model were right.

  3. E(s12)=σ2(1+γ/(n−p1)), so s12 overestimates σ2 unless 𝛃β2=0.

  4. At a new point with regressors (x10,x20), the short prediction 𝛃x10⊤β^1S has bias 𝛃(Π⊤x10−x20)⊤β2 for the mean 𝛃𝛃x10⊤β1+x20⊤β2.

thm-dep-outlier.title: One contaminated response
thm-dep-outlier.html:
Let X have full column rank. For a data vector y, a case k and a shift Δ, let yΔ=y+Δek, where ek is the kth standard basis vector.

  1. The estimate moves by 𝛃𝛃β^(yΔ)−β^(y)=Δ(X⊤X)−1x(k). The fitted vector moves by ΔMek, a vector of length |Δ|hkk. The fitted value of case k moves by Δhkk, and its residual by only Δ(1−hkk).

  2. If 𝛃E(Y)=Xβ and Cov(Y)=σ2I, then 𝛃β^(YΔ) has mean 𝛃β+Δ(X⊤X)−1x(k), and the residual sum of squares has mean σ2(n−p)+Δ2(1−hkk).

  3. Suppose hkk<1, and let 𝛃β^(k) be the estimate without case k. Then for every y, 𝛃𝛃‖X(β^−β^(k))‖2=hkk1−hkk⋅ε^k21−hkk.{#eq-dep-influence}

  4. Under the conditions of (c), adding ek to the model matrix as an extra column gives the coefficients 𝛃β^(k) for X and 𝛃δ^=yk−x(k)⊤β^(k)=ε^k/(1−hkk) for the new column.

thm-dep-overfit.title: Irrelevant regressors
thm-dep-overfit.html:
Suppose 𝛃β2=0, so the short model is correct, but the long model is fitted.

  1. 𝛃𝛃E(β^1)=β1, 𝛃E(β^2)=0 and E(s2)=σ2.

  2. 𝛃𝛃Cov(β^1)=Cov(β^1S)+σ2ΠCΠ⊤. Hence 𝛃𝛃Var(a⊤β^1)≥Var(a⊤β^1S) for every a∈Rp1, with equality iff Π⊤a=0, and 𝛃𝛃Cov(β^1)=Cov(β^1S) iff X1⊤X2=0.

  3. At a new point x0=(x10⊤,x20⊤)⊤, 𝛃𝛃Var(x0⊤β^)=Var(x10⊤β^1S)+σ2(x20−Π⊤x10)⊤C(x20−Π⊤x10), and summed over the design points 𝛃𝛃E‖Xβ^−Xβ‖2=σ2p, against σ2p1 for the short fit.

thm-dep-random-x.title: Least squares for the population projection
thm-dep-random-x.title_html: Least squares for the population projection
thm-dep-random-x.html:
Let (xi,Yi), i=1,…,n, be independent copies of (x,Y), where x∈Rp (whose first component may be the constant 1) and Y have finite fourth moments and Σ=E(xx⊤) is positive definite. Let 𝛃β∗=Σ−1E(xY), 𝛃U=Y−x⊤β∗ and Ω=E(U2xx⊤). Then E(xU)=0, and as n→∞:

  1. 𝛃𝛃n(β^−β∗)→Np(0,Σ−1ΩΣ−1) in distribution;

  2. s2→E(U2) and ns2(X⊤X)−1→E(U2)Σ−1 in probability;

  3. if E(U2∣x)=E(U2) almost surely, the two limiting covariances agree. Otherwise the usual interval for 𝛃a⊤β∗ of nominal level 1−α has coverage tending to 2Φ(zα/2ρa)−1, with ρa=E(U2)a⊤Σ−1a/a⊤Σ−1ΩΣ−1a.
